CT417 Topic Guide

Refactoring and Design Patterns

Identify the concrete design smell, choose a pattern that removes it, and show the resulting structure in code.

What repeatedly appears in the papers

Refactoring/design patterns are a full 20-mark Question 4 in both 2024/25 and 2025/26. The repeated pattern is: explain refactoring, identify a design problem, use abstraction/polymorphism to remove role conditionals, and use a Factory so new roles do not require controller edits.

Rapid refresher

ProblemAppropriate responseDo not claim
Duplicated role-specific methodsExtract common operation to an abstract class/interface; call it through the abstraction.That changing names alone is refactoring.
Repeated if/switch(role) in clientsUse polymorphic subclasses and a creation boundary such as a Factory.That a Factory automatically makes every class open for extension.
New roles require edits throughout the systemDepend on User, not concrete roles; register/inject creators where appropriate.That the example has no remaining extension trade-offs.

How to answer the code subparts

  1. Name the duplicated conditional or responsibility, then state its maintenance consequence.
  2. Show the abstraction, at least two concrete subclasses, and the client using the abstraction.
  3. For a Factory answer, separate creation from use.
  4. Explain the benefit in terms of adding a role or changing a role-specific behaviour.

Practice question - role-based account system (20 marks)

Inspired by: 2024/25 Question 4 and 2025/26 Question 4.

Scenario. CampusPay has Customer and Manager accounts. Its controller contains repeated authentication/account-creation code and branches on a role string. Partner and Auditor roles are planned.

(a) Why is refactoring important for code reusability? [4 marks]

Model answer: Refactoring changes internal structure while preserving externally observable behaviour. It removes duplication, separates responsibilities and makes common behaviour easier to reuse and test. For CampusPay, centralising shared controller logic and delegating role-specific behaviour prevents a fix from being copied into several role methods. It reduces maintenance risk, but tests are needed to show that behaviour has been preserved.

(b) Identify two concrete design problems and a suitable improvement for each. [4 marks]

Model answer: First, the controller’s role conditionals violate open/closed intent: every new role requires editing existing code. Introduce a User abstraction with role-specific implementations and call authenticate() polymorphically. Second, account creation is coupled to concrete classes. Use a Factory/creator boundary so the controller requests a User rather than constructing each role directly. These changes improve extensibility and isolate change.

(c) Refactor authentication so the controller no longer has one method per role. [6 marks]

abstract class User {
  abstract boolean authenticate(String username, String password);
}
final class Customer extends User {
  boolean authenticate(String u, String p) { return validCustomer(u, p); }
}
final class Manager extends User {
  boolean authenticate(String u, String p) { return validManager(u, p); }
}
final class UserController {
  boolean authenticate(User user, String username, String password) {
    return user.authenticate(username, password);
  }
}

Why this earns credit: the controller depends on the abstraction; role-specific behaviour is in subclasses; an additional role can implement User without adding another controller method.

(d) Use a Factory for account creation and explain how to avoid repeatedly modifying the controller for new roles. [6 marks]

interface UserCreator { User create(String username, String password, String extra); }

final class UserFactory {
  private final Map<String, UserCreator> creators;
  User create(String role, String username, String password, String extra) {
    UserCreator creator = creators.get(role.toLowerCase());
    if (creator == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown role");
    return creator.create(username, password, extra);
  }
}

Model answer: The controller calls factory.create(...) and receives User. A new role supplies its subclass and creator registration instead of another controller branch. In a small exam answer, a switch-based Factory can still centralise construction; to make the stronger open/closed argument, use registration/dependency injection as above. The trade-off is that registrations must be configured and validated.

Final check

  • Did I show how the changed code removes a specific duplicate/conditional?
  • Did I distinguish polymorphism from the Factory’s creation responsibility?
  • Did I explain extension in terms of a concrete future role?
